speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is so little
difference between us with respect to some phases of this question that it is rather difficult to understand why the government has not taken the necessary action to liquidate the claims that have been made against this fund. The Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) the other day referred to the fact that the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) was probably prepared and placed in his hands. That is not a matter of very great importance, but I should like him and the house to know that the resolution

was prepared by the hon. gentleman himself, and that with the exception of two or three words which were added in order that the resolution might afford the government an opportunity to pay part of the claims, if it so desired, it represented his views because he was vitally affected owing to the fact that of the 1,613 cases that were considered, some 752 came from Nova Scotia and of those 752 cases, 350 arose in the constituency represented by the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment. You will therefore understand why he is so vitally interested and why he prepared his resolution in the terms in which he did, looking towards the payment by the government of a portion of the claim or at least of those that were, we will say, not large in amount rather than embarrassing the government by pressing for the payment of them all.
The Secretary of State made a rather long statement with respect to the rights under the treaty of those who seek reimbursement out of the fund in the hands of the government. I do not propose to traverse that question. The matter is neither difficult not complicated. The treaty is very clear and plain, the moneys that were derived under the Dawes plan were available for certain purposes; those moneys have been received and they have been paid over. Why has the government kept back the money? Shortly put, that is all there is in the case.
Now let me go a step further. The hon. gentleman also referred to another matter, namely to the different considerations that prevail with respect to the settlement of the claims of the Massey-Harris Company and of the Thompson Steamship Company. Neither of those cases, as he very properly pointed out was similar in character to the cases we are now considering. They arise under another branch altogether of the treaty. The position may be summarized in this form. Germany admitted liability which was limited by the terms of the treaty of peace to injuries or damages sustained by the civil population. As I shall presently show, the government set up a tribunal for the purpose of ascertaining what those claims amount to and they have now considered judgments in their hands as to how those claims should be dealt with. Our contention is that it is their duty to pay over these moneys.
The Secretary of State dwelt at great length upon what he regarded as the legal position of the money and of the government with respect to it. He contended that the money paid under the Dawes plan by Germany- mark you, by Germany!-to this government

Reparations Claims-Mr. Bennett
to satisfy claims of the civil population, be-oause that- is what her obligation is, cannot by an action brought by individuals be taken away from the government. We will admit that at once. No subject may maintain an action against his sovereign, against the state itself unless he obtains a fiat granted as requested by a petition of right. In this instance we have what I shall presently show is a legal claim of every individual affected, but a claim not enforceable in law. Let me take the case referred to by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), namely, the Alabama claims because they bear a striking analogy to this particular case. England denied liability; the matter was referred to arbitration and in consequence of the arbitration a finding was made against England to the extent of some $15,000,000. That amount of $15,000,000 was paid by Great Britain to the United States of America and all individuals, shipowners and others, who were affected, were paid their proportion of the money that was paid by Great Britain to the United States after they had established their claim to the satisfaction of the United States.
There are other cases which are doubtless in the minds of many hon. members where governments have received large sums of money which were available for the purpose of satisfying claims of their nationals or citizens against that fund. It does not of course follow that the citizen can maintain an action to recover any part of that money, or to obtain a judgment against his country in satisfaction of his claim; but there is a claim there, a claim which may not be enforced in the courts of law but which, as I shall presently point out to the house, has been conclusively admitted by the high court of parliament and which waits but one thing, the placing in the estimates of sufficient sums to satisfy the claims of those who have justly established their right to those moneys that were paid to Canada by Germany for the purpose of satisfying the claims of the civil population.
Now if we bear in mind the fact that it has nothing whatever to do for the moment with the enemy property question, except to the extent to which if we did not have sufficient money we might by an act of this parliament make that money available to satisfy these claims, as they have done in the United States, it would seem to me that the difficulties mentioned by the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) would entirely disappear. We have nothing to do for the moment with respect to enemy property, with the custody of alien enemy property; we are not concerned with injuries sustained by the nationals S5103-203
of this country to their property in Germany, nor with any injuries to ships that may have been held by Germany in the Kiel canal, nor with any damages that may have arisen by reason of Germany using them during the war. What we have to deal with are claims made by citizens of this country against Germany for injuries sustained by them as civilians-as civilians-during the war.
Now let us see what our position is, according to the admissions made by the government itself on grounds of high policy. We submit to this house that these moneys are in a sense earmarked for that purpose, that they are available to satisfy these claims, that they came into the hands of this government with a trust imposed upon them, and not as part of the general revenues of the Dominion government. In support of that position, you are not in any sense bound to accept my view, but I do submit that the view of the government, this government, the government of which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. .Lapointe) was then Minister of Justice, the government of which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was then the leader, the government of which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was then a member, is embodied in a statement made by the Hon. E. M. Macdonald, Minister of National Defence, on the 19th of June, 1925. That statement must be taken to be a statement of policy. It is a statement of a member of the government, and according to the well-known principles of cabinet solidarity, there is no question but that that principle enunciated by a responsible minister of the crown as to what the position of this government was in 1925. was accepted, as a matter of fact, by those concerned as being a binding declaration of policy by the government of the country. At page 4522 of Hansard, Mr. Macdonald said this:
I was not in when this resolution was called-
Then he proceeds.
The moneys which come from the Dawes commission, so called, are payable under the terms of the treaty of Versailles for certain definite purposes. They cannot be put into the treasury of the country and appropriated for other purposes than those for which they are paid. The compensation is paid in connection with the following list of cases:
Then follows the list of cases mentioned in the treaty, in what we call the annex, which is similar to a schedule of an act of parliament. There follows this list from the schedule of the treaty of the cases under which compensation will be paid when the money is received from Germany. The Right Hon. Mr. Meighen interrupted Mr. Macdonald at

page 4523 and asked him what his authority was for making that statement, whereupon Mr. Macdonald continued:
This is a memorandum from the Undersecretary of State, and it sets out the clause from the treaty of Versailles which provides the lines upon which compensation can be obtained from Germany and the amount of money that is payable to this country as a result of what is known as the Dawes report, on account of damages arising in these various categories.
That I submit is a correct statement of the situation, made by a minister of the crown, speaking, as all ministers do, the view of the government with respect to the matter then under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It did not impress the house at the time.

I am coming to that. The Minister of Justice is entirely in error as to that. The Hon. Mr. Copp, then Secretary of State, withdrew his resolution, but the resolution was withdrawn for reasons which I think any government would regard as good and sufficient. What was the resolution? The resolution was to pay without knowing what the judgments were, to pay before the commission had reported, and to pay without having before them anything of any definiteness at all. Let us look at what the resolution was. At page 4517 of Hansard, you will find that Mr. Copp's resolution was:
(1)	That the report of the commissioner appointed to inquire into and report upon the claims for reparation of Canadian nationals, upon approval by the governor in council, shall be deposited with the Secretary of State of Canada in his capacity as custodian of alien property.
That report had not been made; the commission had not finished its labours; the judgments had not been concluded; but this resolution was to anticipate all that and provide that when the judgments were made they should be lodged with the Secretary of State. Then paragraph (2) provided:
That from time to time, as sums are received-*
This is vital; this is a recognition of policy. This is a statement of high policy by the government of this country:
(2)	That from time to time, as sums are received on account of reparation under the Agreement of London between the allied and associated powers and Germany, bringing into force what is commonly known as the Dawes plan, the amount thereof shall be paid by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General to the Secretary of State as custodian, until such time as the aggregate of such payments is equal to the total amount of the claims for reparation as determined by the report of the said commissioner and approved by the governor in counoil.
rMr. Bennett.]
If that is not a recognition of obligation and a promise to pay, I would like to know what would constitute a recognition of obligation and a promise to pay. That is so clear that there can be no getting away from it. Then follows the third submission:
(3)	That the Secretary of State shall, on receipt of such payments, from time to time distribute the same to persons found entitled to claims for reparation in the commissioner's report, by way of pro rata dividend.
And then he must lay before parliament his report. In other words, there was a recognition by this government of the fact that the moneys were received with a trust imposed upon them, that they were earmarked to meet certain obligations and liabilities, and that the commissioner was so highly thought of, having been selected by the government itself, that when he made his report, then without any appeal, without any effort at changing it being made, these sums would be paid on the strength of his judgments. That was the position on June 19, 1925, three years ago, within a few weeks. There was a promise made by the government of this country, speaking through two of its ministers, the Secretary of State and the Minister of National Defence, that these obligations would not only be recognized but paid.
But this House of Commons objected to making a promise to pay before judgments were delivered. Sir Henry Drayton objected that the matter was too serious to be considered in the closing days of the session. It is true the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen made observations with respect to payment of property claims before the payment of claims with respect to personal injuries, and other members did the same, but their basis of objection to this resolution was that it put into the hands of the government the power to pay out moneys before the judgments had been delivered, which was in itself a serious departure from principle. In other words, the contention was that the judgments must be delivered, the cases made out before the commissioner, and his report presented to parliament before parliament voted the money, and I shall presently show that upon the application of the very principles that were presented to this house by the opposition at that time, and accepted by the government, these moneys should now be paid.
Let us proceed. That was in 1925. The resolution was withdrawn, and it is a matter of passing interest to know that when the resolution was withdrawn by the Secretary of State he recognized the fact that it was properly withdrawn, for after Mr. Macdonald

Reparations Claims-Mr. Bennett
had made his statement, and after various speakers had presented their views, the resolution was withdrawn by the Secretary of State because, he said, the leader of the opposition and others in their righteous indignation had expressed their views in respect to it. So he clearly recognized that they were right in the contention they made. His words were:
I regret very much that my hon. friends, particularly the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) have risen in righteous indignation because this bit of legislation is brought down in the interest of those who have suffered during the war. If they had the full information that I have and knew the very large numbers of poor people, fishermen particularly, on the different coasts of this Dominion who have suffered-
Sir Henry Drayton: It is a pity the minister would not give us the information.
Mr. Copp: I asked that the resolution be allowed to go into committee, when I would give the information to hon. gentlemen opposite.
Those were the statements of the government, speaking through the Secretary of State, about the suffering that would be imposed upon poor people, particularly fishermen, by this resolution not being passed three years ago.
Now we come to the next year, 1926. There were questions asked in an endeavour to find out what were the facts, but for reasons, which need not be discussed here, nothing was done. But in 1927 the matter was again brought to the attention of this house. I find at page 2218 of Hansard of that year questions were asked by Mr. Stevens with respect to this matter and answered by Mr. Rinfret, in the course of which he reviewed the whole of the circumstances much as he did Saturday. Question 19 asked:
What is the intention of the government with regard to payment of the awards made by the reparations commissioner?
This is the answer:
The policy of the government will be decided when the reparations commissioner has completed his report.
The report is being considered now.

Exactly; and he completed it some months ago. I shall show presently it is more than that. This session again questions were asked by Mr. Manion, and they will foe found at (pages 687 to 688 of Hansard of February 22. 1928. One or two of these questions and the answers thereto I should like the house to consider. This is question 15:

The final question relates to the distribution of the moneys. Now, Mr. Speaker, on February 22, the minister said the report was in the hands of the printer; this is now May 21-three months later. I am credibly informed the report has long since been printed and advance copies of it, in anticipation that it would be tabled, placed in the hands of the pres for release when the moment came. But further than that, sir, I have under my hand the letters written by the Under Secretary of State in February last and of the secretary to the commission presided over by Mr. Friel in which, in answer to questions by claimants as to when the claims would be paid, it is said that the report would be submitted to parliament in a few days. It was fully expected by the Under Secretary of State that it would be so submitted. The minister says the report was in the hands of the printer. I say to the Prime Minister and his cabinet: When a public inquiry has been instituted by the government by order in council under the authority of the governor general in council and the Inquiries Act, and a report is made thereon, that report belongs to this House of Commons, and not to the government. And what is more, Mr. Speaker, we propose to insist that

that report be brought down in. this house. The government may say: You are helpless in the matter; we have our majority behind us, and we will not give the report to you. Well, since the institution of British representative government supply is granted only when grievances are remedied. In- fact governments came into being under British parliamentary institutions for one reason, and one only, that there might be a body of men who would present to the sovereign the grievances of the people as expressed in the House of Commons in order that those grievances might be redressed.
Now, what has happened? I submit we have a condition which this house probably has never seen before. The government, by order in council, appointed a commissioner to investigate claims under a treaty, which treaty was a contract between, among other nations, Germany and Canada. The commissioner has made inquiry and has delivered his report. He is through, he has nothing more to do, he is functus officio. Now parliament is told by the government that it cannot have this report which the country is paying for. Surely the government realizes that that position cannot be maintained.

I thought I made it very plain on Saturday that there was no objection at all to tabling the report, except that the list of names with the amounts opposite might lead a number of persons to conclude that those amounts would be paid to them, when in fact they might not be. Under those circumstances we thought it would not be advisable to lay the report on the table.
You promised to.

I say again there is nothing in the report that we do not wish the opposition to know of. We rather want the opposition to agree with us that it would be inadvisable to lay the report on the table under such circumstances.

The hon. Secretary of
State has made just one mistake in the use of words when he says there is no objection to the opposition having the report. I am not speaking for the opposition, I am speaking for the people of this country who are affected by this report. It is not a question of the opposition seeing the report. It is a question of the rights of this parliament to have before it a document which the people are paying for. It is a judgment delivered by the commissioner, and it should be laid
fMr. Bennett.]
on the table of this house and so be available for the people. What is more, the report was printed by the government for that purpose.
No.
Well, for what purpose?
So that a certain number of copies would be available for members of the cabinet privately to consider the report.

The hon. gentleman did not put that limitation in the answers he gave early in the session, three months ago. This is an afterthought. I can only say this, Mr. Speaker, that we on this side of the house, in view of the situation which has developed, must insist as a condition of supply being granted that we have the report.

that the Prime Minster would endeavour to impose on the house by making the statement that he has just made. The Prime Minister knew when he rose to interrupt me that that was not the report of the commissioner.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING. My hon. friend's remark was that what the Secretary of State said was an afterthought. That has as much to do with the report as a confidential memorandum with respect to naturalization. Ministers prepare confidential reports for council, in order that council may be apprised of that which they have to consider. When that statement was made to induce this house to think that the right hon. Prime Minister held in his hand the report, I say it was all wrong. He had before him a confidential memorandum, prepared probably by the Under Secretary of State, indicating to his minister, and through him to the cabinet, what should be done [DOT] with respect to the report on reparations.
Now let us get down to what is involved in this matter. Here is a report submitted by a commissioner appointed by this house- because the governor in council represents this house, it is the administrative side of government, when parliament is not in session. The cabinet of the country, I say, appoint a commissioner, who is paid to conduct a certain inquiry. That commissioner has submitted his report and, his duties having been performed, he has ceased to function. He has delivered several judgments and submitted a final report, and that report we want. That is all; we have a right to it. And, what is more, it has been promised from time to time. The question has been asked on various occasions by different members as to when the report would be delivered and the government have replied, " In a few days ". But those few days have become weeks and the weeks months, and nothing has yet been done in the matter. There is no necessity for such a delay, and I am sure that if my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) were on this side he would be most insistent that a document, prepared by a commissioner appointed to consider and report upon a matter of such great importance, and upon which the country has a right to know his conclusions, should be presented to parliament in order that it might be dealt with.
Mr. Friel, the commissioner, made his report. Now, it well may be that there are those who consider that these judgments should be reviewed, although no suggestion was made to that effect when the commissioner was appointed. The claims filed amounted to over $50,000,000 and, with interest, to over $75,000,000. In answer to what the Secretary of State has said with respect to the difficulties that might arise from people being led to believe that they would get a larger sum than they might afterwards receive, it is only neoessary to point out that the commission granted only $4,000,000 without interest, instead of $50,000,000 with interest, or a total including interest of less than $7,000,000-$7,000,000 as against $75,000,000. Obviously therefore he was not overgenerous.
Does my hon. friend take the stand that the report should be considered as final?

The amendment moved by the hon.
member for Queens-Lunenburg reads as follows:
"This house regrets the refusal of the government to introduce legislation at the present session of parliament providing for the payment in full or in part of the various sums fixed by James Friel, Esquire, K.C., a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act, as losses sustained by the civilian population of Canada during the great war."
In support of that amendment, if I understand him correctly the leader of the opposition advanced the following argument: First, there is no legal liability on the part of the government, or there is no legal claim on behalf of any citizen of Canada in connection with any of these claims.
I said there was no enforceable claim.
It is not enforceable because it is not legal.

No, it is like a petition
of right. You cannot sue the crown.
I would not like to misquote my hon. friend. Does he contend that these people have any claim at all?

Certainly. I read what
Mr. Macdonald said, that the receipt of this money imposed a trust upon the government to pay the claims, but inasmuch as no claim may be made against the crown it is not enforceable. That is the whole point.

Mr. Macdonald's statement covered altogether different grounds. If the leader of the opposition takes the position that there is a legal claim, his argument is quite different from that made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Calian) on Saturday afternoon, when he declared in the most positive manner that he admitted there was no legal claim. The contention of the leader of the opposition is 
altogether different from the argument brought forward in the British House of Commons by the then Chancellor of the Exchequer, Right Hon. Austen Chamberlain, who maintained that there was no legal claim in connection with these matters. The argument of the leader of the opposition is also different from and foreign to the stand taken by every one of the governments concerned with these claims, and I do not think my hon. friend seriously contends that any of these claimants have what we call a legal claim against the government in connection with these matters. The hon. gentleman went on to say that the moneys received under the Dawes plan were received by this government for one purpose, the purpose being to pay the civilian claims in connection with war losses; that in consequence these moneys, so to speak, were earmarked; that the government had only one thing to do, and that was to use those moneys for the purpose for which they were paid by Germany and to compensate these Canadians for the losses sustained.
Where does the hon. gentleman get his authority? After all, behind any assertion in this house, no matter how positive it may be, must lie some authority to support that assertion. Where is it? Where is the support for my hon. friend's assertion that this is a trust? Where does he find it? I am very much surprised when I hear that the hon. gentleman does not rely on outside sources, and says that the whole of his claim rests on the authority of Mr. Macdonald, who was Minister of National Defence for some time in the Liberal government.
Is not article 232 sufficient authority? May I read it to you?

But the minister says, oh this position was vacant before on one occasion right after the war, in 1920. Cooper was an applicant then but was not accepted at that time. The position was given to a man by the name of Fenwick. That I know is what the minister has in his mind, or part of what he has in his mind. So in that connection I should like to quote to him from a statement of the Civil Service Commission on that particular point. They say:
In this connection it might be pointed out that the material under consideration at the time of Mr. Fenwick's selection-
That would be in 1920, I think:
[DOT]-was entirely of a different nature to that in the present competition. The circumstances surrounding Mr. Cooper's candidature in 1920 were also different inasmuch as he had no place to keep the post office at that time, and was competing against an applicant who lost a son overseas.
That did not give him any preference.

This son had won the D.C.M. and prior to enlistment was his father's chief help on the farm. The father, as a consequence, and on account of poor health being unable to get along without his son, was obliged to sell his farm and move to the village.
Those were the circumstances in 1920. The commission continue:
In the present instance, Mr. Cooper offers a suitable accommodation and location for the post office, and is certified by the inspector as being qualified in all respects. The examining branch, therefore, has no alternative but to recommend his appointment.
That is dated March 23, 1927. In 1920 when Cooper applied for the position, Mr. Fenwick, who had lost a son in the war and was obliged to abandon his farm on that account, applied for the position of postmaster, and
Supply-Post Office

the sympathy of the community went out to Mr. Fenwick. Because of that fact, and of the further fact that Cooper at that time had no place for the post office, a decision was given in favour of Mr. Fenwick. Now the Postmaster Generali seeks to excuse his action by referring to the report of the Civil Service Commission in 1920 as indicating Cooper's lack of qualifications for the position. It does not indioate anything of the kind. The inspector certified that Cooper had the qualifications. The Postmaster General may say that he is not a very good writer. Well, I had a note from the Postmaster General the other day, and a letter from Cooper some time ago, and having taught school for some years, and therefore being somewhat of a judge of handwriting, I would give Cooper more marks than I would the Postmaster General.
What would you do about your own handwriting?

Well, I can write better than you; you may bet your life on that. But the Postmaster General gave another reason for turning against Cooper. He said:	Oh, this man Cooper is
in debt. Now, I ask him if he really thinks he should have put that in? Does the Postmaster General really think that because this returned soldier owed a couple of hundred dollars, this should be advanced as one reason why he should not have the position? Will he answer yes or no?
You will get your answer at the right time.

All right, I shall wait for the answer with interest. I refer to that now as one of the reasons advanced by the Postmaster Generali why this man, who had served his country in the war, the only one of the seven applicants-

Does the hon. gentleman
state there were seven applicants?

Yes, and I vill give you their names. They were: P. J. Murphy, W. S. Fenwick, 0. B. Jackson, Geo.
Cooper, Miss Wiseman, W. P. Covert and Mrs. Lockwood.
Where did you get the information?
From your own department. That ought to be good enough.

No.
I.Mr. J. W. Edwards. I

Yes. If you will look over your files you will see that is correct. Apparently the minister wanted to see only one name in this connection. He had made up his mind that he was going to have efficiency, according to his ideas. Efficiency was the only thing that counted with him. He declared: I am determined, though the heavens fall-
Oh, oh.

I am determined, says the Postmaster General; no matter what happens, law or no law, Civil Service Commission or no Civil Service Commission, I will have my way in running this department; I will dismiss postmasters by the hundred for the efficiency of the service, because Liberal members of parliament say it will be more efficient to put out a man who voted on the Conservative side and give the position to one who voted Grit. That is his estimate of what constitutes efficiency. He estimates efficiency in the public service by the way a man votes at elections. He may be the biggest numskull on earth, but if he votes Grit, then according to the standard of the Postmaster General he is efficient. Now, I should like to get an answer to that question.
You will get it after you are through.

Well, it is said the pleasures of anticipation are greater than those of realization. I do not subscribe to that theory. However, we will have to wait. I have another case, but I will leave it in cold storage for a little while.
Oh, come on.
I know the hon. gentleman-
You are not going to let him answer before six.
I think it is better to keep everything in chronological order. The other is the Odessa case. Probably the minister will remeber Odessa. I wrote a letter about it.
I remember it quite well. That is where you certainly did all you could to support the returned soldier.

We shall see when we come to it. Apparently the hon. gentleman has made up his mind, but we will

Supply-Post Office
see if we cannot change it. It is a pretty difficult thing to do. Now I come 'back to this Enterprise case. Don't forget, Mr. Postmaster General-

speechtext: Order.

-you can answer me in any order you wish, but don't forget that I asked you if you thought you were playing the game square by putting up the excuse against this man Cooper that he was slightly in debt.
I did not say slightly.
You said he was in debt. If you have the information as to the amount of the debt perhaps you will give it.
Even if I had I would not give it to the hon. member.

Did I understand my hon. friend to say he would not give it to me?
Some hon. MEMBEiRS: Sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I do not
believe my hon, friend has the information as to the amount.
You may be quite correct,-
Yes, and in other things too.
-and you may not.

I hope my
hon. friend does not go so far as to say that ho will not give an answer to my question whether or not it was proper for him to mention the fact against Cooper that he was in debt as one reason why he should not have the position. The Postmaster General will not deny that he made use of that argument. Now I ask him if he thinks that is just square.
Go on till six.
Carried.
Go on.
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, the item is
not going to carry yet awhile; we have a few other questions we wish to ask the minister. As a matter of fact I think he should answer the question that has just been put to him. Possibly he thinks five minutes to six does not give him sufficient time.

It is four minutes to six.
Had the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) stopped at ten minutes to six he would have given me an opportunity.
Call it six o'clock?

I should like to have it
called six o'clock, but I wish to assure my hon. friend I do not need that time to collect my thoughts and reply to him. I have the goods right here.
If the Postmaster General is not prepared to go on presumably he wants further time to consider this matter.
No.
Mr. Chairman, the Postmaster General can sidestep as much as he likes, but there is no doubt he wants a little time to look over things and prepare himself before he speaks.
If the house will give unanimous consent to sit until five minutes after six, I will handle the hon. gentleman. I have called your bluff.
I am rather surprised-
You are.
I am rather surprised-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Wait a moment. I am rather surprised at the Postmaster General's tactics. It is not in my power to change the rules, but so far as I am personally concerned I am ready to sit here until eight o'clock to give an opportunity to answer.
Sit down.
Call it six o'clock.

No.	I
thought the hon. gentleman was going to proceed. I intimated that so far as I am concerned he could go ahead. I am ready to sit here until five minutes after six or five minutes after seven.
Call it six o'clock.

No, we are
not going to close until six o'clock.
Go ahead.

The other
day in the house when another matter was under consideration I referred to the fact that
Supply-Post Office

the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) had given the preference, in the case of an appointment, not to a returned Canadian soldier but to a returned British soldier. The hon. gentleman passed a note across the floor to me asking to what office I referred when I made that statement. I wrote on the bottom of his note, which I passed back, the word "Odessa". The matter that was being discussed then was preference to soldiers. The man who was appointed postmaster of Odessa is, I believe, well qualified for his position; there were several others well qualified also. But the fact is that this man who was appointed to the post office there did not become a resident of Canada until after the war. He came here from the old country after the war, having served in the British army, though not at the front. However, he performed in the British army such service as they thought him best qualified to discharge. Under our interpretation of the law-and I have no fault to find with it personally-he ranks as a returned soldier. There were however returned soldiers, Canadian-born, among the applicants.
Six o'clock.

Not quite; it lacks about a quarter of a minute. Now, while I would draw no hard and fast line between returned soldiers born and brought up in England and returned soldiers born and brought up in Canada, at the same time, other things being equal, I am free to say that I should be disposed to give the preference to a Canadian soldier who was born and raised in this country. I shall be glad to receive the information I asked for when the minister has had time to prepare it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six o'clock we were considering vote No. 20 on page 9 of the estimates.

When the committee rose at six o'clock the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington had been discussing the question of the appointment of a postmaster at Enterprise. He and I had previously discussed the Ottawa promotion, and I think perhaps sufficient has been said in that connection unless further information is required by the committee, which I shall be glad to give.
In connection with the postmaster at Enterprise let me point out that the hon. mem-

ber for Frontenac-Addington got a little ahead of the blows which he expected to deliver in connection with that appointment in 1921. This office became vacant in that year through the resignation or death of the postmaster, at the moment I forget which. Three applications were received for the appointment. I interrupted the hon. member this afternoon and asked him if he were not mistaken as to the number of applicants, thinking he was referring to the appointment in 1921. He was right when he said there were six or seven applicants for the position in 1927. In 1921 the report of the inspector touching upon these three men, of which I have both a copy and the original, was as follows:
Cooper has no place to keep the office, and no means to purchase a building, but his foster father states he will buy one for him. Fenwick on the other hand, owns the premises where the office now is, which is well adapted for the purpose, so no change in site would be necessary if he were appointed.
Both are highly spoken of and there does not appear to be anything against the character of either, but I am bound to say that Fenwick is much the better appearing man of the two, and more fitted for the position. In fact, were it not that Cooper had been overseas, he should not be considered, because he lacks the attributes which the former possesses.
That was the report submitted by the qualifying inspector sent to rate the different applicants. Later on this office became vacant again through the death of Mir. Fenwick, who received the appointment in 1921 through a certificate issued by the Civil Service Commission. That was a case of a civilian being appointed as against a returned soldier, but I have yet to learn that the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington, who to-day stands up as the champion of returned soldiers and who at that time was a member of the government, if I am not mistaken, never raised his voice on behalf of Cooper. In fact, I know he did not.

When was
that?
That was in 1921, when my hon. friend was a member of the government.

What time
in 1921?

I have not the exact date.
I see I was mistaken; it was in 1920 that the vacancy occurred through the resignation of Mr. Wagar. My hon. friend may not have been a member of the government, but he was a leading member of his party at that time. I do not know that he ever raised his voice on behalf of that returned soldier, and he never had anything to say about it until Mr. Fenwick died in 1926. I was then in

Supply-Post Office
charge of the Post Office department and applications were asked for, six or seven being received. Among the applicants was this returned soldier, George A. Cooper, the only returned soldier who applied. The inspector who acted in 1920 was again called upon to qualify these applicants for the position, and his report reads as follows:
George A. Cooper is a returned soldier, and on this account has a lot of sympathy from many residents. He does not appear to be very bright and states he is barely able to make a living at his work. He is a tinsmith and does odd plumbing jobs. His education is lacking. ... It was also ascertained that he was in debt. Mr. Cooper was an unsuccessful applicant for this position six years ago.
When this report was placed before me I went back over the record of Mr. Cooper, and I felt that if he were lacking in education, as is stated in both reports, and in the attributes necessary for such a position as the first report states-
That is not what the report said.

It stated he lacked the
attributes possessed by the other gentleman.
That is very different.

The other gentleman possessed the attributes which qualified him for the position, and if Mr. Cooper did not possess the attributes which the other gentleman had certainly he did not possess the attributes necessary for the position. That is a roundabout way of saying it, but that is the fact.

My hon.
friend's logic is very bad.

It is bad for my hon. friend; no logic presented from this side of the house can rind favour with him. We know that, so we do not try to impress our logic upon him. May I further add that in addition the inspector reported that if this man had not been a returned soldier he would not have been in the running at all, and this official, working under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, whose duty it was to state all the facts in his possession, further said that this man was in debt. Under those circumstances I felt it my duty to refuse the certificate from the Civil Service Commission, and I did so.
Might I ask a question? Did the man who made that report serve in the war?
I do not know; I cannot tell my hon. friend that.

He served in the Tory
party, did he not?

He was appointed by the Tory party. I do not know that being a returned soldier would help him in making a report of this kind. However that might be, the hon. member for Frontenac-Adding-ton stated that I had appointed or named another individual to take the place of this man. That statement is not correct. While the minister has the power to direct his deputy to refuse a certificate-it can only be done through his deputy

the minister has not the power to name a person in the place of the one whose certificate was refused. The refusal of the certificate goes back to the commission and they make their choice from among the other applicants. In this case there were six applicants, and when the commission received the refusal by the department of their certificate they chose the next one who should receive the certificate. That certificate was issued and it was accepted, and that is the whole story.
While I am on my feet I will refer to the case brought up by the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) regarding the appointment to the position of postmaster at Odessa. I might just mention that there are two post offices of this name in the Dominion, one out west and one in the hon. gentleman's riding. The postmaster died and, if I am not mistaken, his son continued to act until the commission could appoint a permanent official.
It was not his son, but a man of the same name.

In looking over the records I find that the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington was not so anxious to stand up for the returned soldier as he is standing up for him now. There were four returned soldiers applying for the position at Odessa, one of whom was a disability man. If my hon. friend were as honest then in his advocacy of the rights of the returned man as he pretends to be now, he certainly would never have written the letter he did on August 4, 1926, when the shadow government was in power. What do I find in the official records of the department? I find this letter dated at Kingston, August 4, 1926, addressed to L. J. Gaboury, deputy minister of the department:
My dear sir:
I understand that several persons have applied for the vacant postmastership at Odessa.
He knew there were several applying.
I visited Odessa yesterday and made most careful inquiries into the situation there and after mature consideration beg to recommend the appointment of Mr. S. W. Clark for the position. Mr. Clark's son, Percy, has been in the office for the last year and a half and

Supply-Post Office
during the past six months has had full charge of this important office. He is competent, courteous and popular with all. If he was 21, I think there would be no question as to this appointment which I feel sure would please the public. He is only 18-[DOT]
I want you to listen to this, and see what my hon. friend wanted to do with this important office.
He is only 18 and I ask for the appointment of his father, who is well qualified to discharge the duties of the office, and who would be the responsible one. He would no doubt retain the services of his son, who has discharged the work so satisfactorily, as your inspector will testify. ' This is a very important office-
And yet he wanted to put a boy of 18 in charge of it !
This is a very important office, and I am anxious to have it properly filled.
If you please!
I beg to request that you will give my representations your favourable consideration and that you will show this letter to the Hon. Dr. Manion.
I do not know whether he did that or not.
I remain,
Yours truly,
J. W. Edwards.
Was that a civil service job?

His party was in power and they did not care about the Civi'l Service Commission. Now that they are in opposition they are very solicitous for the rights of the Civil Service Commission.
But what do I find? I find that Melville G, Lee was an applicant, a returned soldier. D. O. Frink was an applicant, a civilian. Stanley J. Smith was an applicant., a returned man. W. C. Snider, civilian; R. A. Hamon, civilian; Roes D. Schermeshorn, a returned soldier with disability, and S. F. Hillier, a returned soldier, were also applicants.
_ When the present government came back into power, and after these advertisements were put out, it was reported to the department that there were two other returned soldiers who desired to have the opportunity of applying. The report of the inspector on the qualifications of those who had already applied had not been received, and I wrote the Civil Service Commission that it would please the department if they would consider the two additional applicants and allow them to apply, and have the inspector look into their qualifications. This was done, and among others who applied was the returned soldier whom the hon. gentleman referred to this afternoon as being an imperial soldier, having been only four or five years in Canada. On the report of the inspector as to his quali-

fioations, approved by the commission, this soldier received the appointment certificate of the commission. When the certificate came to me, feeling that preference should be given in all cases to Canadian soldiers I took the matter up with the commission. There were Canadian soldiers applying, and my hon. friend knew that when he recommended that a young boy eighteen years of age be put in charge of this office. I received a reply from the commission that I had misinterpreted the act. They said that under the act any soldier who had served in any of the commands of the British colonies, and who afterwards came to Canada, would have the same preference as a Canadian soldier. They told me that that was the interpretation of the act. My feeling is that if that is the interpretation, then the act should be changed. Preference should be given to Canadian soldiers in all cases, and not to soldiers belonging to the allied British colonies; it is a privilege that should belong to Canadian soldiers and Canadian soldiers alone. The Civil Service Commission, however, ruled against me, and I had nothing to do but accept their ruling. I will frankly confess that if I could have found a good reason which would have justified my refusing the certificate of that soldier, which was given to him in preference to a Canadian soldier, I would have done so. But I could find no reason, because the law was against me.
We thought you were more resourceful.
I am resourceful, in so far as it is necessary to be resourceful to do what I consider to be fair and just.
Why did you not make it a bilingual position?

Because I knew my hon.
friend opposite would raise the race cry. My hon. friend is too good a sport not to take his medicine. He will have his turn and then I shall have mine, which I will take advantage of, to come back at him. Let me go one step further. I should like the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington to explain this to the committee:	How is it that when his
party are in power, they do not care a snap, as this letter proves, for the returned soldier; but when they are in opposition my hon. friend is the champion of the returned soldier? We hear him to-day fighting in parliament the battles of the returned soldier, but when the occasion arose when he could have done something for the returned soldier, he was as dumb as an oyster and he did not do any-

Supply-Post Office
thing. Where is the consistency of my hon. friend? I do not think I have anything more to say on those two points; I think I have said enough just now to give my hon. friend reason to think over the position in which he has placed himself, and if any more questions come up I shall be only too glad to deal with them.

I can assure the committee and the Postmaster General that I shall not require two hours to get my thoughts into some kind of order. In regard to the Enterprise post office, to which the Postmaster General has alluded, I took up the cudgels, if I might use that word, on behalf of Cooper. The Postmaster General has corroborated what I said this afternoon in regard to Cooper. He has added to what I said. He said that the inspector, who was the same man in 1920 as in 1927, spoke of Cooper as being highly regarded in the community, but he laid considerable stress on the fact that the inspector said that Cooper did not possess the attributes possessed by Fenwick. By a peculiar line of reasoning, or logic, if I might dignify it by that term, the Postmaster General says that the inspector, by saying that Cooper does not possess the attributes which Fenwick possesses, has thereby said that Cooper does not possess the attributes necessary to fill the office. That does not follow at all. I will concede at once that Fenwick was a better qualified man than Cooper, but the records and statements of the inspector in 1920 and 1927 in regard to Cooper indicate positively that Cooper did possess all the requirements necessary to fill the position efficiently.
Why was he not selected?

I gave the
reason and my hon. friend also gave the reason. I will give this illustration to show the Postmaster General how absolutely ridiculous what he would dignify with the name of logic is. The position of postmaster is vacant. Two men apply for the position. The inspector reports that both men are qualified. One man, however, is a university graduate; he certainly has qualifications, and his attributes are superior to those of the other man, but the other man possesses all the qualifications required to fill the position.

And he was a returned
soldier.

Very well,
take it that way if you like. The returned soldier in this case was Mr. Cooper. The
inspector reports that Mr. Cooper possesses all the qualifications that are required to fill the position efficiently. Mr. Cooper's educa-tonal standing is not as high as that of Mr. Fenwick. Therefore the Postmaster General reasons that he does not possess the necessary attributes at all. That is contrary to the report of the inspector. The reason why Cooper was not selected in 1920 was given by the commission and I read it this afternoon. There is no need to read it again. The reason was mainly that he did not have any place in which to hold the office and consequently the preference was given to Fenwick-not because of Fenwick's superior qualifications, because both were qualified, but because Fenwick owned the place where the post office had been for twenty years and furthermore because of the fact that he had lost a son in the war and was obliged to give up farming on that account. Those were the reasons which influenced the commission in 1920.
But does the act not state that the preference shall be given only to a returned soldier and not a civilian who may have lost a son in the war?

It is quite true that the act does not take into consideration the fact that a civilian applicant for a position may have lost a son in the war, but that is what influenced the commission in 1920. I submit to the judgment of the committee whether or not the Civil Service Commission was doing its duty at that time. The minister says that I did not in 1920 appeal on behalf of Cooper. If I understood the minister aright, in 1920 there were three applicants for the position, namely, Fenwick, Cooper and some other person.
Mr. VENIOT. A woman, Mrs. Lockwood.

I may say
very frankly that no letter was written to me in regard to the matter and I know why the request was not made. I know that by visiting the place since, in 1926 and 1927. The reason was that the general opinion of Grit, Tory and everybody else in that community was that the position should go to Fenwick because of the sympathy, rightly placed or not, which they had for him on account of his having lost a son overseas. That is the explanation in regard to that.
I take up the other matter, the matter of the Odessa appointment. The minister says that I wrote a letter asking that young Clark be appointed to the position. That is very true. I did write a letter. The minister said
Supply-Post Office

that I was not at all concerned at that time about relieving a returned soldier, a well-qualified man who was born in Canada and who went overseas with the Canadian forces. I want to inform the minister-and his files will show that I am correct-that the point he is endeavouring to make falls to the ground because at that time neither Frink nor Lee had applied.

Frink is not a returned
soldier.

No, he is
not. But Lee is a returned soldier and I will mention how the thing happened.
What about the other returned soldiers who had applied?

The other returned soldiers, as the minister will know by looking at his files, were reported by the inspector as not being qualified, with the exception of Pooke. That is that. I want to say just why I interfered on behalf of Clark. The minister spoke about this letter requesting efficiency and then he threw his arms up in the air and said that I was willing to allow this important office to be filled by a boy of eighteen. If that applies to me, what about the minister himself? He apparently was willing to let the boy fill the office and the boy did fill the office until September 15, 1927, when Pooke took charge. Though the minister holds up his hands in holy horror at the very thought of this boy of eighteen carrying on in this office, trying to make a point out of the fact that I recommended the boy, nevertheless he is so perfectly satisfied with the boy's efficiency that he allows him to carry on in the office for months and months afterwards.
Why did I write my letter on behalf of Clark? I will give the reason. The Civil Service Commission were notified of the vacancy on July 9, 1926. Let me say that the postmaster in Odessa had for nearly a year before that date been a sick man, and this young fellow of the same name, though not his son-I do not know whether they aie related in any way-had carried on and been fully responsible for the duties of the office during that year in which the postmaster was sick. After the postmaster died, young Clark still carried on. and carried on apparently with perfect satisfaction to the Post Office department and to everybody else concerned for about a year and a half.
As I said, the Civil Service Commission were notified of the vacancy on July 9, 1926, and applications were asked for in the early part

of July to fill the vacancy. Quite a number of .persons applied, and a date was fixed when these applications would be considered and an appointment made. Here is a list of those who applied, given in order of merit:
W. C. Snider, not a soldier.
R.	A. Hamm, not a soldier.
S.	W. Clark, not a soldier.
That is one, two, three, in order of merit, as reported by the district superintendent. The fourth in the list was W. J. Pooke, the man who was later appointed, an overseas man. Then came Smith, then another man by the name of Snider, then Schermeshom and Hillier. Hillier, by the way, being from Peterborough, was shut out because they said that they were going to give the office to somebody in the locality. Up until that time, August 6-my letter was written on August 4 -neither Lee nor Frink were applicants for the position. As a matter of fact, Frink was a very active politician, and pressure was brought to bear on the minister that Frink should be given a chance to apply for the position. I will remind the minister that on November 24th, which was quite a long time after my letter was sent in, the Postmaster General asked the Civil Service Commission to reopen the case and call for new applications in order to give D. O. Frink the opportunity to apply. I said at that time that if the opportunity was to be open for Mr. Frink, who was not a returned soldier, it should also be open for Melville Lee, a Canadian and a returned soldier, whose application had not gone in in the first place. When the government failed to make the appointment after the expiry of the time when the applications were to be considered, as nothing was done I went up to Odessa, which is only a few miles from my home, and made inquiries from the people there, irrespective of party-some of them applicants themselves-about the filling of the position. I venture to say that two-thirds of them said this: "Can't you let this young fellow Clark keep on? Everybody is satisfied with him. He is popular, very courteous and obliging."

Would the hon. member
please tell us whether this Clark family were Liberals or Conservatives?

I realize, of course, that from the hon. gentleman's standpoint, if I said they were Conservatives that would condemn them, but if I said they7 were Liberals they would be in the proper category, m his estimation. I perfectly appreciate the fact that so far as the hon. gentleman is con-

Supply-Post Office
terned there is only one way, as I said this afternoon, which he and others have for measuring- the efficiency of a man for any position, and that is by his politics.
Now answer the iuestion.

Having obtained the views of the community, having learned that they wanted young Clark to remain on if the government would allow him to do so, I wrote my letter to the department, which had failed to make any decision on the applications they had received

I must correct my hon.
friend. The department does not make the decision; it is the Civil Service Commission.

Well then, the Civil Service Commission. The Civil Service Commission had not made any decision up to that time. I believed that it was in the interests of that community, and that it was what the people of that community wanted, that this young man should carry on. There was only one way in which that could be done, and that was through the appointment of his father until the young man should reach the age of twenty-one. His lather had had considerable experience as assistant in the post office, and was a thoroughly competent and thoroughly responsible man. That is the reason I made the recommendation. But let me point out that at that time as the file of the minister will show some of those who applied for the position and others I could mention said that this man Pooke should not be given the appointment because he was not a Canadian.
That is right.

That is the attitude which they took. I am net taking that attitude, but I do say that when the vacancy was reopened at the request of the minister for Frink, Lee should also have been given the opportunity to apply at the same time. I say that Lee was just as competent ?n every respect as Pooke. I should like to know if that is still the practice of the department?
We do it in some cases.

I should like to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the case of Mr. Hermenegilde Picotte of the town of Penetanguishene, who for thirty years carried the mail to and from the station. The contract price was very low and during the whole thirty years of his service he gave

Supply-Post Office
every satisfaction both to the public and to the department. But being a free citizen he is supposed to have voted for me at the last election.
That is a sin.

That is a sin, yes, and a punishable sin too. When his contract was about to expire this spring, the Liberal executive of the town called a meeting in the office of the defeated candidate, and said that because this man had voted for Thompson, Thompson would have to find him a job. So the defeated candidate called upon the Postmaster General not to renew the contract but to call for tenders. This was done and another man was given the contract at a lower price. I want to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that Picotte, who for thirty years had been a faithful servant, is incapacitated by certain disabilities from doing any other work. I have a medical certificate from his doctor under date of March 12, 1928, which states:
This is to certify that I have this day examined Mr. Herman Picotte, and find him ill from the following: Chronic bronchial asthma; high blood pressure, from hardening of arteries; chronic (marked) varicose veins of both legs.
The Postmaster General smiles, I may say for his further amusement that this man suffers so badly from asthma that he has not been able to sleep in bed for the last twenty years. He cannot do any other work, but with his horse he was able to carry on this service to the satisfaction of the public and of the department. Because, however, in the exercise of his right as a free citizen he voted for me, he must be punished and in his old age thrown out of employment. His condition might not be so pitiable were it not for this fact. When war broke out he had two sons both of whom enlisted voluntarily. One son was rejected as being physically unfit, but the second son, Napoleon, enlisted as a private in the 157th Battalion, giving up a good position in the Grand Trunk or the Canadian National service. He was successively promoted from private to corporal and from corporal to sergeant. He received the meritorious conduct medal for bravery on the field of action, but unfortunately one day he was killed in France. He did not come back to support his aged father and now a grateful country turns this man out into the cold.

The same discussion took place in the house last year that is taking place to-night. I remember taking part in it and advocating the increasing of the salaries of postal clerks and railway mail carriers by $120. It was stated by the Postmaster
General that certain classes of the civil service had previously received increases and he could not see why he should grant them to all. In view of the fact that such an increase would mean a satisfied department in face of the increased cost of living I advocated that the increase of $120 be made general, but at that time the Postmaster General refused to grant or to recommend any increase. He said that he would recommend a reclassification. What difference does it make what classification they are in? What could you call a railway mail clerk, except a railway mail clerk? I could not for the life of me see what other name you could give them; they would still be railway mail clerks. I do not think the Postmaster General is very anxious in the matter, but the government should certainly take some action.

The fact that there can be a reclassification of railway mail clerks is evidenced by the fact that the Civil Service Commission is mow considering, on the recommendation of the Postmaster General, a readjustment and reclassification of railway mail clerks by grading them so as to put them in a class where they will get a greater salary than they are receiving to-day.
It is not a difficult job to regrade them, but you cannot call them anything except railway mail clerks.
Yes, you can.

You cannot call them
butchers. You are just passing the buck.
Would the Postmaster General be good enough to inform me why the practice of his department was not followed out in the case which I have cited?

If the non. gentleman had called my attention to this matter before I would have been in a position to give him the information, but he cannot expect me to carry in my head the reasons for everything that takes place in the post office. I will get the information and give it to him to-morrow.

I have perused the recommendations and correspondence relative to this question of increased salaries for railway mail clerks. The letter of the 2nd May from the secretary of the Civil Service Commission to Mr. Gaboury, Deputy Postmaster General, sums up the situation, but it does not convey the idea which the Postmaster Genera! conveyed to the committee a moment ago. The letter states:
I am directed to advise you that at a meeting of the commissioners this morning the recommendation for increased compensation for
Supply-Post Office

the classes letter carriers, mail porters, postal clerks and railway mail clerks, was given very careful consideration by the commission, and that their decision is that there should be no increase granted in the basic rate for those classes.
I want to ask the Postmaster General two things. Legally and according to the act, is the method of getting an increase that of effecting a reclassification, that is, changing the terminology of the employment, or is it by a straight increase in compensation of the different classes specified here?
An increase in the minimum and maximum, and therefore carrying with it a yearly increase greater than in the past until they reach that greater maximum.
That would be a reclassification.
It is both; that is the way I look at it, but perhaps I may not be using the right term. If the hon. gentleman will just read the first part of that letter-

I quote:
I am directed to advise you that at a meeting of the commissioners this morning the recommendation for increased compensation

Increased compensation.
There is the direct recommendation.

Quite so, but I would judge from that paragraph that there is no authority to grant it, and that you have to do it in some other way. I am asking if there is any other way by which the same result can be achieved.
No, because if there had been, they would have pointed it out.
They did so.
Where?
In the next paragraph.
Read it, please.

I want the Postmaster
General to mark carefully the distinction between these paragraphs. The one I have read says that there should be no increase granted in the basic rate for these classes. The next paragraph says:
The commissioners, however, believe there is ood reason for considering the suggestion made y your department some time ago that some change should be made in the class of railway mail clerk to provide for increased compensation for the clerks in charge of railway post offices, and would be pleased to receive from the department their views regarding how this provision could best be effected.
That paragraph really indicates that the responsbility is passed back to the minister. What has he done to effect an increase?
Let us get the record right. The first paragraph refers to mail clerks, postal helpers and letter carriers-
And railway mail clerks.
One moment, please. They deal specifically with the first three classes, leaving out the railway mail clerks.

They do not. I have read it. I will read it again. It says:
Letter carriers, mail porters, postal clerks, and railway mail clerks.
They are all mentioned in the first paragraph, so how does the ministers' explanation work out?

It would work out, because they specifically in the next paragraph pick out mail porters, mail clerks, and so forth, and they drop the railway mail clerks and later deal with them specifically and say, "In the oase of railway mail clerks, we may reconsider it, because we believe so-and-so, and we would ask you to suggest how it could be done." We have submitted to the Civil Service Commission a proposition of regrading, or grading, if you will, the railway mail clerks. They dismissed the first three entirely.
So far as basic rates are concerned.
I got in touch with the Civil Service Commission, or my deputy did, and we discussed the interpretation of that clause. The result agrees with what I say now.
What did they say?

They say they will not
recommend any increase.
In what?
For the mail clerks, mail porters and the other class, just as it is in that letter. The hon. gentleman has the advantage of me; he has the document.
More than that, they say the basic rates.

A delegation of railway
mail clerks went to the Civil Service Commission and discussed the whole matter with them. They came to me and asked my permission, as Postmaster General, to allow them to discuss the matter with the Civil Service Commission. I granted that; there could be no objection. They went. They returned to me, and they told me that the Commission had told them that they were there as the watchdog of the treasury.

Supply-Post Office
When did this take place7
After the 3rd of May, and they did not care what my recommendations were in that respect, they could not grant the recommendations for increases.
The Postmaster General will note that his suggestion is quite inconsistent with paragraph 2, where they invite him to make recommendations.
Only in regard to railway mail clerks.

Certainly; that is the
subject matter of my comment.
They refused to consider the first three classes, but in the case of the railway mail clerks they asked us to make a suggestion to them.
The minister knows that they did not refuse increases for the first three classes. They only refused the basic rate.

The basic rate is the whole thing. The moment you increase the basic rate and raise the maximum, you are giving to the service the right to annual increases greater than they receive to-dav. If you do not touch the basic rate it is no use touching anything at all. I am perfectly safe on the ground I am taking. I want the committee to understand that I am not trying to crawl out of anything. I am not trying to make any capital out of the fact that I did make a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission and they did not accept it. I merely wish to state the facts as they are. I may be wrong in my interpretation, but I feel I am not; I have had experience in dealing with this matter for a few years.

I would like to test the bona fides of the minister right here and now With respect to paragraph 2, where the commission invite the minister to make a recommendation for increases in salaries to the railway mail clerks, will the minister make that recommendation as requested?

That question is very easily answered. I made it eight days ago. Will that satisfy the hon. gentleman? My deputy can give the exact date, but on my instructions he went to the Civil Service Commission and discussed the matter with them. There was a delegation of the railway mail clerks present in my own office; we discussed the matter with them and agreed with the railway mail clerks what their increase or readjustment should be, and we brought that to the attention of the civil service commission. It is now in their hands to act upon it.

As we have gone so
exhaustively into the question, will the minister not produce the letter and put it on the record?
My deputy tells me that he will produce the document. I have not got it here. We have nothing to hide. I will produce anything that I can get in the department.
Do I understand that this letter is a recommendation from the Postmaster General to the Civil Service Commission?
Not from the Postmaster General-from the deputy under my instructions. It is practically the same.

It is virtually from the Postmaster General recommending to the Civil Service Commission an increase in salaries with respect to the railway mail clerks as indicated in the second paragraph of this letter of the 2nd of May?
Yes.
Where do the watchdogs of the treasury come in? How are they going to bark?
I do not know. So far as the watchdogs are concerned, I am simply-reporting to you what the delegation reported to me.

From what the minister has stated, I believe that he is quite anxious that all these postal employees, as w^ell as the railway mail clerks, should get $120 per annum more than they are getting at the present time. There has been a fairly unanimous expression of opinion in this house on that matter this evening, and all parties have indicated a desire that that increase should be given. In view of that expression of opinion, I wouid ask the Postmaster General again to make this request of the Civil Service Commission for an increase. If he does that, and the Civil Service Commission again turn it down, we will know exactly where we stand. If the Postmaster General does that, I am sure the members of the house will be obliged tc him.

I may say for the information of the committee that the government desires to get another department into supply this evening in order to take up an item or two, and when I have finished answering my hon friends I shall move that the committee rise and report progress.
In answer to the hon. gentleman, as an evidence of good faith of what the department desires to do, I may State that I brought
Supply-Post Office

the matter before council, and after consideration of the increases of the salaries of these classes an item of $350,000 was slated for the supplementary estimates; but when the Civil Service Commission replied as they did on May 2, that item was withdrawn. It will not now appear in the supplementary estimates unless the commission reconsider their decision and accept our recommendation.
Will you ask the Civil Service Commission to reconsider their decision?

The hon. minister has stated in his last few remarks what purports to have occurred in council, We have on many occasions, and probably this afternoon, inquired as to certain facts or alleged facts, and the answer invariably was that anything that occurred in council could not be divulged. How does the hon. gentleman square himself with that position? As a matter of fact he is giving this information ostensibly for the benefit of the suffering public but really for political purposes.

My parliamentary experience in the commons has not been as lengthy as my hon. friend's, and I may have forgotten myself in that respect. I admit that perhaps it was a breach on my part, but I think I was doing nothing but right in laying the facts before the committee.
I have an idea that the hon. gentleman knew perfectly well what he was doing. He was doing it for the purpose of affecting votes in the country.

The Postmaster General is quite frank. He believes in the spoils system, and makes no pretence about it whatever. The Post Office department is supposed to be operated for the benefit of the country, not for the benefit of this or. any other political party, but there has been politics in the department since confederation. I know that in the Toronto post office a man cannot get a temporary position at Christmas unless he joins the Liberal party. I have Seen the list. Who is in control regarding appointments; is it the Civil Service Commission? No, the Civil Service Commission has no more to do with it than the man in the moon. The list is presented to the postmaster, and he must act on it. If the returned soldiers do not vote Liberal they are dismissed, and their places are taken by others who will vote Liberal. The whole thing is ridiculous. That is not the way to operate a public utility. I do not say the present Postmaster General is entirely to blame; I think he stood by the men. I wish to put in a word for the low-paid men in the Toronto post office, the post-

men and others. Some of these men were in France for four and a half years. Day after day they have hard beats to walk. They give the maximum of efficiency at the minimum of pay, and there is no public utility using its men in the larger cities the way the low paid men of the Post Office department are used to-day. The Post Office department would have a large surplus were it not for the Special rates given to the newspapers, which is equivalent to a cash bonus of seven million dollars. This is given at the expense of the rank and file of the Post Office department, who are getting a miserable pittance of a salary to-day. Some of these men drawing only $700 or $800 are delivering registered mail containing hundreds of thousands of dollars in value. Are we to wait until there is another strike in the post offices throughout the country? The men are long-suffering and patient, and they have put up with a lot from the Civil Service Commission. Last year we had to wait three or four months before we could get this return. I never heard of so much red tape as exists in the Civil Service Commission over the classification of these men. They are a splendid body of men giving excellent service to the public at very low remuneration. I say from the top down they are underpaid. Take the Toronto post office; Mr. Lemon, the very capable head, is paid only about $5,800 a year, although the revenue from that office is six million dollars a year. The rank and file work long hours and are underpaid, and we should do something to relieve the conditions under which they labour to-day.
Item stands.

10.

That is immigration and
colonization. I do not think it is in order to call another department without reporting progress on these estimates, when there would be a motion to go into committee again.

Supply-Immigration

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If there is any objection we can take up some other item, but we wish to get the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) into supply to-night.
Immigration and Colonization - salaries, $305,570; contingencies, $45,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speechtext: Before proceeding with a discussion of the vote I want to offer a word of explanation. Some time ago, discussing the question of immigration, the leader of the opposition requested that we give the estimates in a more detailed form than we have them on page 22. This has been done, and a more detailed statement will be distributed to-morrow. On page 22 of the estimates it will be found that the whole vote is contained in six different items. We have divided it up into a great many items to make it more easily understood by hon. members, and to-morrow the details will be distributed. As regards the vote now before the house, my deputy is not here, but I may say that the total vote this year for civil government, salaries, is 8305,570 in comparison with $279,920 for 1927-28. This makes a total increase in the vote of $25,650. The explanation of this increase is the number of employees for the present year. This increase in numbers is accounted for as follows: 1 chief of records; 1 head clerk; 1 principal clerk; 16 clerks, grade four, promoted from grade three. This makes a total of 19, less 4 of a net decrease in lower grades due to adjustments and promotions. The estimated amount for 1928-29 is $305,570 as compared with $265,850, the amount voted for 1927-28, plus a flat increase of $120, which was granted under vote 535, which brought last year's total up to $279,920. This means that the increase for 1928-29 amounts to $25,650.
What are the duties of a commissioner of immigration?

There are three commissioners. as explained to the committee the other day. There is one in Vancouver, there is one in Winnipeg and another resident in Ottawa. These are called division commissioners. The Commissioner of Immigration is superior to these, having control of the whole Dominion from sea to sea.

I do not see the three
commissioners mentioned this item. What are the duties of a commissioner of immigration? What does he do to earn his money?

He has the whole question
of immigration under his care. Perhaps one of his most important duties is the supervision of the different ports. Any difficulty arising in Quebec or Halifax where immigrants enter the country is immediately attended to by the immigration commissioner. Internal work is under his supervision.
And what are the duties of a commissioner of colonization?

The Commissioner of Colonization is more particularly associated with the settling of immigrants after landing in Canada. He also has under his control the different agencies in the United States, but as his title implies he is more particularly connected with the settling of immigrants after they have landed in the country, in contradistinction to the' Commissioner of Immigration, who deals with them only in so far as their entry is concerned.
Progress reported.
